author: implementer
content: All 41 text I/O calls in the four scoped files now pass encoding="utf-8" (orchestrator.py 29, review-package.py 8, session_start.py 2, stop_guard.py 2). os.open at orchestrator.py:191 is deliberately excluded: it creates a raw descriptor for the task lock and passing encoding= to it is a TypeError. The os.fdopen calls that wrap descriptors in text streams (lines 165, 204) were given the encoding.

author: implementer
content: Text-mode write_text translates newlines as well as encoding it: with no newline= argument it writes CRLF on Windows and LF on Linux, so every generated artifact has platform-dependent line endings. Observed directly -- the ADR bytes are 'Supersedes:** \xe2\x80\x94\r\n'. A whole-file byte-equality assertion against text.encode('utf-8') therefore fails on Windows for reasons that have nothing to do with encoding; my first draft of test_requirement_text_round_trips_through_task_creation failed exactly this way and was narrowed to assert on the encoded characters. This is pre-existing and outside TASK-006 scope, so it was left alone. It is a real separate defect and a candidate for its own task.

author: implementer
content: _support.py still has unencoded text I/O: write_state, read_state, write_plan, write_requirement and events all call read_text/write_text with no encoding. The plan does not declare _support.py so it was not touched. The test harness therefore writes fixtures in the locale encoding; the suite passes only because every fixture is ASCII. Any future test needing a non-ASCII fixture written through TaskDirCase must fix this first.

author: implementer
content: A behavioural test alone cannot catch an unencoded-text-I/O regression, because on a UTF-8 host the locale default is already correct and the call passes. test_utf8_io keeps a static AST audit alongside the round-trip tests for this reason. The audit was checked against a known-bad baseline (git show HEAD:.ai/scripts/orchestrator.py) and reported 7 of 7 calls missing encoding=, confirming it discriminates rather than always passing.

author: implementer
content: The constitution lists .ai/scripts/ among the paths the implementer must never write, but plan v1 declares .ai/scripts/orchestrator.py and review-package.py in files_to_modify -- the task is about those files. I treated the approved plan's explicit declaration as the authority, per the standing rule that workflow infrastructure is writable when the plan declares it. Flagging it because the two rules read as being in tension; the resolution should be deliberate rather than assumed.

content: Scope-check warning for the orchestrator: plan v2 declares 4 files_to_modify + 1 files_to_create, but this session modified and created none of them, because v1 had already brought all five to the state v2 describes.
